title: Learning: conditioning and observation
note: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus comes to predict a stimulus that already triggers a reflex. In operant conditioning, consequences change how often a behavior occurs: reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it. 'Positive' means something is added and 'negative' means something is removed.

read.title: Positive, negative, reinforce, punish
text: Operant conditioning has a vocabulary that trips up many students, but two questions sort it out. First, is the behavior becoming more likely or less likely? If more likely, the consequence is reinforcement. If less likely, it is punishment. Second, was something added or taken away? Added is positive; removed is negative. Neither word means good or bad.

So a child who earns a sticker for reading gets positive reinforcement: something pleasant is added, and reading increases. A driver who buckles up to silence the seatbelt alarm gets negative reinforcement: an annoying sound is removed, and buckling increases. A student scolded for texting receives positive punishment, while a teen who loses phone privileges receives negative punishment.

Timing and pattern matter too. Rewarding every response teaches a new behavior fastest. Once a behavior is learned, rewarding it only sometimes keeps it going, and an unpredictable number of responses, a variable-ratio schedule, makes behavior especially hard to extinguish. That is the pattern of a slot machine.
Researchers generally favor reinforcement over punishment. Punishment can suppress a behavior without teaching a better one.
